title: Korean Murder Cases: Public Opinion Turns Individual Cases into Political Labels
dek: The Chinese student case flipped from "Koreans killing Chinese" to a suspect of Korean-Chinese ethnicity; the police officer who took the report in the Jeju four-body case allegedly fabricated the closure reason. What truly warrants vigilance is not public safety, but how public opinion turns individual cases into political labels.
why: Medium information density, but it provides a more rigorous Chinese-language timeline based on Korean police statements and surveillance footage than Chinese social media versions, suitable for those needing to quickly calibrate their judgment.
who: Chinese-speaking readers interested in Korean society, Chinese students and professionals in Korea, and those who want to follow social media gossip but need a reliable timeline.
skip: If short on time, the latter part of the Jeju case discussing Jeju tourism and infrastructure can be fast-forwarded without affecting the main case narrative.

points.h: The crime time was misreported across Chinese media
points.body: Many Chinese internet reports said the girl went to Jeong's home at 2 PM on August 20; Korean surveillance shows she actually entered with Jeong at 2 AM on August 20. About 20 hours later, Jeong left wearing her clothes and carrying her suitcase, took a taxi to Dongdaegu Station, turned off her phone, changed back into men's clothes in the restroom, and returned, creating the illusion that the girl had left. Police used this route to identify him, and the so-called boyfriend's report did not change the investigation.

points.h: The same Korean-Chinese identity serves different agendas on both sides
points.body: When the case first broke, many on the Chinese internet assumed it was Koreans killing Chinese, worrying it was a hate crime against Chinese. After the suspect was revealed to be Korean-Chinese, the narrative shifted to Chinese killing Chinese. Korean right-wingers and some netizens used it to claim Chinese people enter Korea to kill and that the Korean government indulges Chinese people, also saying the suspect's imprisonment is eating Korean taxpayers' money. The same fact is exploited differently on both sides: Chinese public opinion wants to confirm Korean exclusion of Chinese, while Korean public opinion wants to confirm the threat of Chinese immigrants.

points.h: Calls for deportation are wishful thinking: even a death sentence won't be carried out
points.body: Korea theoretically retains the death penalty but has not executed anyone in about 30 years; even if Jeong is sentenced to death, he won't be executed. Under the principle of territorial jurisdiction, the case is handled by Korea. Extradition to China requires the consent of Korea, China, and the individual himself, and he obviously won't agree. More realistically, he may serve decades in a Korean prison and then be deported, by which time the Chinese internet will have long lost interest. Thus, online calls for deportation are more wishful thinking.

points.h: The closure reason was fabricated by the responding officer
points.body: Jang Mi-ran left home on the evening of May 12 and never returned. Three days later, her cohabiting boyfriend reported her missing. The officer who took the report, surnamed Bu, told colleagues he had contacted her, that she was safe and wanted to be alone, and the search was canceled. Two months later, a new report was rejected because there was a record of "person found." Later, the family reported to Seoul, which ordered a reinvestigation, and the body was only discovered on August 24. After reviewing records, it was found that Officer Bu never actually spoke with her; the closure reason was fabricated by him.

points.h: This is not a one-off mistake but a habit of closing cases
points.body: Officer Bu had been in the missing persons unit for about a year and a half, handling 298 cases. Media reported at least 10 were closed with the method of "person found, wants to be alone." He was also found to have left fingerprints in a female restroom at the police station and was suspended on August 11. Another case of a 60-year-old man was also handled by him and similarly closed as "the person wanted to be alone." The total number of missing person reports in Jeju is not abnormal, but in his case, the proportion and method of suspicious closures exceed normal range and require case-by-case review.

points.h: The suicide theory is hard to accept, but the evidence has already decayed
points.body: The body was found at the edge of a palm grove. For over 100 days, farmland nearby was cultivated daily, yet no one noticed. Media reported she hanged herself, but palm trunks are brittle, and the road to the site at night had no streetlights and was full of potholes. Jang had previously said the grove was scary and she wouldn't go near it; her home was only 400 meters away. These details make the suicide theory hard to fully accept, but the body was highly decomposed, and beyond a neck fracture, no further evidence could be extracted.

points.h: According to police theory she was dead, yet her phone turned on four days later
points.body: If, as police speculate, Jang died the night she disappeared, her phone was last turned on at 9:44 AM on May 16 at Hallim Port, about two kilometers away. This signal falls within the two-kilometer radius between her home and the discovery site. More troubling, surveillance footage after her disappearance could have been checked, but because Officer Bu had already closed the case, by the time the investigation was reopened, the footage had been overwritten, leaving only the initial footage of her leaving home. The missing evidence chain makes it hard to re-investigate and leaves room for various speculations.

points.h: Conspiracy theories lack evidence; procedural failure is the real issue
points.body: Korea ranks first in OECD suicide rate, while intentional homicide rate is only moderate. Therefore, Jeju police's inclination to classify the four bodies as suicide is not entirely baseless given the data and remaining forensic evidence. The problem is that key evidence disappeared due to the initial erroneous closure, and police tend to close cases quickly, which amplifies conspiracy theories. Currently, there is no direct evidence for mafia, murder maniacs, or police protection; the most concrete accusation is procedural failure.

I think it's still that saying: it's not as good as we think, nor as bad as we think. Right. Many people say you have to analyze specific situations; every place has crime.

Because I think a lot of the information on X and TikTok cannot be trusted. Last night I saw some big bloggers on X posting about these cases; some of them specialize in posting news. I feel what they post is problematic. Because they don't understand Korean, but they grab it from elsewhere.

We might be relatively slower, not that fast. And we won't appear particularly aggressive; without very sufficient evidence, we won't say anything definitive, right? But at each time point, we help everyone sort out what has actually happened so far. I think that's very important.
